title: Yesterday's concert: rehearsing by phone and the tambourine
summary: Albert explains the planned list for the new master of ceremonies, phone rehearsals with Freddie Coleman, Walter Lewis and Cottrell, three-part harmony on two numbers, and the tambourine as a link to the slaves.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, you did. I mean, it seemed to me yesterday at the concert that you had everything planned and you knew when we were talking about.

I did. I did. Because this is a different incident altogether. What we're talking about. We're talking about playing dances in the olden days. Well, you had a set format because you went to a different city every night. And possibly sometime you'd stop in a city maybe for two weeks and that was considered a big contract. And two weeks, man, we really had a rest. But yesterday, you're referring to yesterday at the concert, the reason why I had a list made is because of the new master ceremonies that was there. What was his name? Mel Levin? Mel Levin. In the past, Plato Smith has been the master ceremonies. I was just trying to familiarize him with the program. I didn't know you hadn't noticed that.

Well, I'm trying to notice everything, you know. Well, that's great. You're inquisitive. You told me about how nothing was rehearsed yesterday. That amazed me because the band, you know, everything was so pretty. All the hominis seemed right to me, you know.

Right. Well, we rehearsed but not at the place. We rehearsed over the telephone. Oh. How did I do that? Yeah. Okay. I discussed it with Freddie Coleman. I told him, I said, you know what I want you to do, don't you? What? I said, well, I want you to do the same thing that you did last year. Bring that tambourine and watch my tempos. Well, I tell you to cut him and cut out and just listen to me. And he laughed. He says, okay. So, I did the same thing with Walter Lewis, but Walter had just recently played a concert with me in San Antonio and he was familiar with most of the numbers. I just had to set him in the spots where I wasn't going to play him. And the same way with Cottrell. And plus, he, well, he's just a good man.
So, you had no problem. It's just the guys worked together. Right. And they knew that I could play three-part harmony if you wanted them.

Right. Well, you noticed the three-part harmony on Mood Indigo, the three-part harmony on Look Down at Lawson Road, which was the only ones that required a three-part harmony. The others was go as you see or as you feel.
And you used the tambourine just on one moment?

Well, the tambourine, yes. Because the tambourine was fitting into the story of jazz where it began with the slaves. And the slaves played the tambourines. That was one of the only instruments they could play. And finally, from there to maybe the guitar and then modulated on to the way it is now. And the tambourine was to give it the sort of a holy roller effect, as we call it. The way the slaves used to go from one thing to the other. That's why I was trying to tell Mel, you know, as much as I could, so he would go ahead and use his own words.
